JavaScript String Length
The length property returns the length of a string:

let text = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";

let length = text.length;
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Extracting String Characters
There are 4 methods for extracting string characters:

items: Using property access [] like in arrays

blocks.text: JavaScript String charAt()

The charAt() method returns the character at a specified
index (position) in a string:

let text = "HELLO WORLD";

let char = text.charAt(0);
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: JavaScript String charCodeAt()

The charCodeAt() method returns the code of the character
at a specified index in a string:
The method returns a UTF-16 code (an integer between 0 and 65535).

let text = "HELLO WORLD";

let char = text.charCodeAt(0);
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: JavaScript codePointAt()

let text = "HELLO WORLD";

let code = text.codePointAt(0);
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text: JavaScript String at()
ES2022 introduced the string method at():
The at() method returns the character at a specified index (position) in a string.
The at() method is supported in all modern browsers since March 2022:

const name = "W3Schools";

let letter = name.at(2);
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text:
const name = "W3Schools";

let letter = name[2];
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text: The at() method is a new addition to JavaScript.
It allows the use of negative indexes while charAt() do not.

const name = "W3Schools";

let letter = name.at(-5);
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text:
const name = "W3Schools";

let letter = charAt(myString.length-5);
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text: Browser Support
at() is an ECMAScript 2022 feature.
JavaScript 2022 is supported in all modern browsers since March 2022:
Property Access [ ]

let text = "HELLO WORLD";

let char = text[0];
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text:
Property access might be a little unpredictable:

  It makes strings look like arrays (but they are not)
  If no character is found, [ ] returns undefined, while charAt() returns an empty string.
  Propert access is read only, but str[0] = "A" gives no error in "sloppy mode".

blocks.text: JavaScript String concat()
concat() joins two or more strings:

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text:
The concat() method can be used instead of the plus operator.
These two lines do the same:

text = "Hello" + " " + "World!";

text = "Hello".concat(" ", "World!");
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text:
All string methods return a new string. They don't modify the original string.
Formally said:Strings are immutable: Strings cannot be changed, only replaced.
Extracting String Parts
There are 3 methods for extracting a part of a string:
JavaScript String slice()

slice() extracts a part of a string and returns the
extracted part in a new string.
The method takes 2 parameters: start position, and end position (end not included).

let text = "Apple, Banana, Kiwi";

let part = text.slice(7, 13);
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text:
JavaScript counts positions from zero.
First position is 0.
Second position is 1.

let text = "Apple, Banana, Kiwi";

let part = text.slice(7);
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text:
let text = "Apple, Banana, Kiwi";

let part = text.slice(-12);
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text:
let text = "Apple, Banana, Kiwi";

let part = text.slice(-12, -6);
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text: JavaScript String substring()
substring() is similar to slice().

The difference is that start and end values less than 0 are treated as 0 in
substring().

let str = "Apple, Banana, Kiwi";

let part = str.substring(7, 13);
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text:
If you omit the second parameter, substring() will slice out the rest of the
string.
JavaScript String substr()
substr() is similar to slice().

The difference is
that the second parameter specifies the length
of the extracted part.

Warning
The substr() method is deprecated in the latest JavaScript standard,
but is still officially defined in Annex B of the ECMAScript specification for backward compatibility.
You are strongly advised to use substring() or slice() instead.

let str = "Apple, Banana, Kiwi";

let part = str.substr(7, 6);
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text:
If you omit the second parameter, substr() will slice out the rest of the
string.

let str = "Apple, Banana, Kiwi";

let part = str.substr(7);
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text:
If the first parameter is negative, the position counts from the end of the
string.

let str = "Apple, Banana, Kiwi";

let part = str.substr(-4);
blocks.caption: Example

A string is converted to upper case with toUpperCase():
A string is converted to lower case with toLowerCase():
JavaScript String toUpperCase()

let text1 = "Hello World!";

let text2 = text1.toUpperCase();
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: JavaScript String toLowerCase()

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: JavaScript String isWellFormed()

The isWellFormed() method returns true
if a string is well formed.
Otherwise it returns false.
A string is not well formed if it contains lone surrogates.

let text = "Hello world!";

let result = text.isWellFormed();
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text:
let text = "Hello World \uD800";

let result = text.isWellFormed();
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text: Lone Surrogates

A lone surrogate is a Unicode surrogate code point that is not part of a valid surrogate pair
used to represent characters in UTF-16 encoding.
JavaScript String toWellFormed()

The String method toWellFormed()
returns a new string where all "lone surrogates" are replaced with the Unicode replacement character (U+FFFD).

let text = "Hello World \uD800";

let result = text.toWellFormed();
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text: JavaScript String trim()
The trim() method removes whitespace from both sides of a string:

let text1 = "      Hello World!      ";

let text2 = text1.trim();
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: JavaScript String trimStart()
ECMAScript 2019 added the String method trimStart() to JavaScript.
The trimStart() method works like trim(), but removes whitespace only from the start of a string.

let text1 = "     Hello World!     ";

let text2 = text1.trimStart();
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Browser Support
trimStart() is an ECMAScript 2019 feature.
ES2019 is supported in all modern browsers since January 2020:
JavaScript String trimEnd()
ECMAScript 2019 added the string method trimEnd() to JavaScript.
The trimEnd() method works like trim(), but removes whitespace only from the end of a string.

let text1 = "     Hello World!     ";

let text2 = text1.trimEnd();
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Browser Support
trimEnd() is an ECMAScript 2019 feature.
ES2019 is supported in all modern browsers since January 2020:
JavaScript String Padding

ECMAScript 2017 added two new string methods to JavaScript: padStart()
and padEnd() to support padding at the beginning and at the end of a string.
JavaScript String padStart()
The padStart() method pads a string from the start.
It pads a string with another string (multiple times) until it reaches a given length.

let text = "5";

let padded = text.padStart(4,"0");
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text:
let text = "5";

let padded = text.padStart(4,"x");
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text: The padStart() method is a string method.
To pad a number, convert the number to a string first.
See the example below.

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: JavaScript String padEnd()
The padEnd() method pads a string from the end.
It pads a string with another string (multiple times) until it reaches a given length.

let text = "5";

let padded = text.padEnd(4,"0");
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text:
let text = "5";

let padded = text.padEnd(4,"x");
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text: The padEnd() method is a string method.
To pad a number, convert the number to a string first.
See the example below.

blocks.text: JavaScript String repeat()
The repeat() method returns a string with a number of copies of a string.
The repeat() method returns a new string.
The repeat() method does not change the original string.

let text = "Hello world!";

let result = text.repeat(2);
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text:
let text = "Hello world!";

let result = text.repeat(4);
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text: Syntax
string.repeat(count)
Parameters

rows:
Required.
The number of copies wanted.

blocks.text: Return Value

rows: A new string containing the copies.

blocks.text: Replacing String Content

The replace() method replaces a specified value with another
value in a string:

let text = "Please visit Microsoft!";

let newText = text.replace("Microsoft", "W3Schools");
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: The replace() method does not change the string it is called on.
The replace() method returns a new string.
The replace() method replaces only the first match
If you want to replace all matches, use a regular expression with the /g flag set. See examples below.
By default, the replace() method replaces only the first match:

let text = "Please visit Microsoft and Microsoft!";

let newText = text.replace("Microsoft", "W3Schools");
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text:
By default, the replace() method is case sensitive. Writing MICROSOFT (with
upper-case) will not work:

let text = "Please visit Microsoft!";

let newText = text.replace("MICROSOFT", "W3Schools");
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: To replace case insensitive, use a regular expression with an /i flag (insensitive):

let text = "Please visit Microsoft!";

let newText = text.replace(/MICROSOFT/i, "W3Schools");
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Regular expressions are written without quotes.
To replace all matches, use a regular expression with a /g flag (global match):

let text = "Please visit Microsoft and Microsoft!";

let newText = text.replace(/Microsoft/g, "W3Schools");
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text:
You will learn a lot more about regular expressions in the chapter JavaScript Regular
Expressions.
JavaScript String ReplaceAll()
In 2021, JavaScript introduced the string method replaceAll():

text = text.replaceAll("Cats","Dogs");

text = text.replaceAll("cats","dogs");
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text:
The replaceAll() method allows you to specify a
regular expression instead of a string to be replaced.

If the parameter is a regular expression, the global flag (g) must be set, otherwise
a TypeError is thrown.

text = text.replaceAll(/Cats/g,"Dogs");

text = text.replaceAll(/cats/g,"dogs");
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: replaceAll() is an ES2021 feature.
replaceAll() does not work in Internet Explorer.
Converting a String to an Array
If you want to work with a string as an array, you can convert it to an array.
JavaScript String split()
A string can be converted to an array with the split() method:

text.split("")     // Split on characters

text.split(",")    // Split on commas

text.split(" ")    // Split on spaces

text.split("|")    // Split on pipe
blocks.caption: Syntax

blocks.text:
let text = "Hi fox!";

const myArr = text.split("");
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text:
let text = "The quick brown fox.";

const myArr = text.split(" ");
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text:
let text = "The quick brown fox.";

const myArr = text.split();
blocks.caption: Examples

blocks.text: Using split("") Can be Unsafe
Using split("") is unsafe for strings containing emojis or complex characters.
The method splits by UTF-16 code units and will break surrogate pairs.
split("") is always unsafe for emojis. It will slice right through them and create broken, corrupt code fragments.
split(" ") is usually safe for words, even if they have emojis inside them, as long as the emoji is not glued right next to a space you are splitting on.
Summary of Options:

items:
text.split("") is most unsafe
It breaks up 4-byte emojis (like 💩 becomes ['\uD83D', '\uDCA9']).

Spread  [...text] is partially safe:
It works for simple emojis like 💩 or 🔥, but destroys complex emojis like 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦, 🧑‍⚕️ (doctor), or flags.

Intl.Segmenter is 100% Safe:
It handles every emoji, accent, and complex characters.

blocks.text:
let text = "👨‍👩‍👧‍👦";

const myArr = text.split("");
blocks.caption: Examples
